scope_note: Family-recognition backfill centered on green Central Texas root hemiparasites so the learner does not overfit Orobanchaceae to pale achlorophyllous broomrapes. Uses Castilleja indivisa and Buchnera americana as primary structural anchors, with Castilleja purpurea / C. lindheimeri as regional paintbrush comparisons.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: First recognize that many local Orobanchaceae are completely green. Look for a root-hemiparasitic herb with simple exstipulate leaves, a bracted spike/raceme, a fused tubular often bilateral corolla, usually 4 stamens, a superior ovary, and a many-seeded capsule.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Green hemiparasitic herb + bracted spike + sympetalous tubular/zygomorphic flower + 4 stamens + superior ovary + dry many-seeded capsule. In Castilleja, much of the showy color is in floral bracts rather than the corolla.
core_characters: Most modern Orobanchaceae are root hemiparasites or holoparasites; green foliage does not exclude the family.
Haustorial attachment is below ground and usually not a practical field character; do not uproot plants just to prove parasitism.
Leaves simple, without stipules, often opposite but alternate leaves occur in Castilleja.
Inflorescences commonly racemose/spicate and strongly bracted.
Corolla fused, usually tubular and bilateral, commonly 5-lobed/bilabiate.
Stamens usually 4, often didynamous and epipetalous.
Ovary superior, syncarpous, generally with many ovules.
Fruit usually a dry capsule with many very small seeds.
Many family members darken or blacken when dried or bruised; useful supporting clue, not a primary diagnostic.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach Orobanchaceae as leafless, pale, or non-photosynthetic; Castilleja and Buchnera are green hemiparasites.
Do not teach leaves as always opposite; Castilleja indivisa has alternate leaves.
Do not assume the bright red/orange parts of paintbrush are petals; they are largely colored bracts.
Do not use visible host attachment as a required field character because the haustoria are underground.
Do not distinguish the family from Plantaginaceae or Lamiaceae by corolla shape alone; parasitic biology + ovary/capsule/seed framework matters.

fastest_cues: Terminal dense spike with conspicuous colorful leaflike bracts.
Actual corolla is narrower and less visually dominant than the bracts.
Four stamens arranged in two unequal pairs.
Capsule many-seeded and often persists inside dried floral parts.
Leaves may be alternate rather than opposite.
Castilleja.teaching_anchor: Castilleja indivisa is the best bract-versus-flower lesson and a clean green hemiparasite example.

fastest_cues: Green rough/hairy herb with opposite sessile leaves.
Terminal spike of dark purple to blue-purple flowers.
Corolla trumpet-like with 5 abruptly spreading lobes.
Plant tissue commonly blackens markedly after bruising/drying.
Capsule oblong with many tiny seeds.
Buchnera.teaching_anchor: Buchnera americana is the best local counterexample to the idea that Orobanchaceae must look like Castilleja or like a pale broomrape.

fast_key: Green plant with showy red/orange 'paintbrush' spike -> inspect closely: if colored parts are bracts surrounding narrow tubular flowers, think Castilleja.
Green rough opposite-leaved herb + terminal spike of purple tubular flowers that darken/blacken -> Buchnera framework.
Tubular bilateral flower + 4 stamens but no parasitic/hemiparasitic evidence and a Penstemon-style staminode -> reconsider Plantaginaceae.
Square aromatic stem + opposite leaves + 4-lobed ovary/nutlets -> reconsider Lamiaceae.

parasite_lesson.field_rule: Hemiparasites photosynthesize but also tap host roots for water/minerals and sometimes carbon. Holoparasites depend far more completely on hosts and often lose chlorophyll.
parasite_lesson.safety_and_conservation_rule: Do not pull up paintbrushes or bluehearts to demonstrate haustoria. Teach the belowground connection with a diagram or published root image instead.
best_visual_sequence: diagram of root haustorium attached to host root

bract_lesson.key_point: The showy red/orange/yellow portion of Castilleja is dominated by modified leaves/bracts, not broad petals.
visual_sequence: circle the narrow actual flower emerging above/inside it

Plantaginaceae.confusion: Both may have tubular bilabiate flowers, 4 stamens and capsules.
Plantaginaceae.tie_breaker: Orobanchaceae is parasitic/hemiparasitic in the modern circumscription and often has very numerous tiny seeds; local Penstemon commonly adds a conspicuous staminode and is not parasitic.

Lamiaceae.confusion: Opposite leaves and bilateral tubular flowers can overlap, especially Buchnera.
Lamiaceae.tie_breaker: Lamiaceae usually has square aromatic stems and a deeply 4-lobed ovary producing 4 nutlets; Orobanchaceae has a normal superior syncarpous ovary and many-seeded capsule.

Scrophulariaceae_old_sense.confusion: Older Texas sources often still label Castilleja/Buchnera as Scrophulariaceae.
Scrophulariaceae_old_sense.tie_breaker: Modern molecular classification places the parasitic/hemiparasitic lineages including Castilleja and Buchnera in Orobanchaceae; preserve old labels as historical source context only.
